source: Vahdati et al. (2026) The ARC of Progress towards AGI: A Living Survey of Abstraction and Reasoning
finding: Survey table of ARC-AGI-1 public-eval scores by paradigm. Spread inside one paradigm is larger than the gap between paradigms. So the way a method is built matters more than induction versus transduction as a label.
numbers: Induction 2% to 79.3% (SD 27.4 points) vs mean between-paradigm gap about 15 points. Survey text: pure transduction caps near 40%, pure induction 79%, hybrids 80-94%. Rows: Greenblatt GPT-4o induction 35.6; Berman 77.1; Pang 75.0; ArcMemo 52.0; SOAR 47.1.
limits: Secondary survey; rows mix 100-task and small subsets and different splits. Survey itself says systems run on all 100 tasks average 38.8% vs 65.6% for <100-task subsets (inflation).
agent_relevance: Do not trust a single headline paradigm number. Compare arms on the same item set at equal tokens, as our rules say.

source: Vahdati et al. (2026) The ARC of Progress towards AGI: A Living Survey of Abstraction and Reasoning (cost and parallelism section)
finding: Frontier reasoning-model cost fell 390x in a year, but the survey says this is mostly fewer parallel samples, not cheaper reasoning. Test-time samples are the big lever, and program-synthesis systems reach similar scores at far lower cost.
numbers: o3 low-efficiency: 1,024 samples, 5.7B tokens per 100 tasks, 87.5% ARC-AGI-1, about $4,500/task. o3 high-efficiency: 6 samples, 33.5M tokens per 100 tasks, 75.7%. GPT-5.2 Pro 90.5% at $11.64/task; Gemini 3 Flash 84.7% at $0.17. Berman evolutionary NL-program system 79.6% at $8.42/task; Pang library system 77.1% at $3.97/task. ARC-AGI-2: Berman 29.4%, Pang 26.0%, GPT-5.2 Pro 54.2% at $15.72; Poetiq Gemini 3 Pro refinement 54% at $30.57; Opus 4.5 37.6% at $2.20.
quote: cost reduction appears to be driven largely by reduced parallelism
limits: Lab-reported semi-private scores relayed by a survey. It does not say whether o3 or GPT-5.2 internally induce programs or output grids, so this is not a clean induction-vs-direct comparison.
agent_relevance: Cost bar for a propose-and-test scaffold on ARC-AGI-1: roughly $4-12 per task is competitive. Every paradigm loses 2.5-3x on ARC-AGI-2.

source: Vahdati et al. (2026) The ARC of Progress towards AGI: A Living Survey of Abstraction and Reasoning (abstract and success-factor table)
finding: Survey lists success factors: multiple candidate hypotheses checked against demonstrations, guided search, per-task adaptation appear in every system above 70%. Program synthesis, neuro-symbolic and neural methods all drop 2-3x from ARC-AGI-1 to ARC-AGI-2.
numbers: Opus 4.6 93.0% on ARC-AGI-1, 68.8% on ARC-AGI-2, 13% on ARC-AGI-3 (abstract). Test-time adaptation 20-30 points over frozen baselines (cites Akyurek 2025). Multi-representation systems 20-30 points over single-representation (survey claim, not controlled). Guided search 72-80%; unguided rarely above 30%.
limits: Correlational summary across different systems, not an ablation.
agent_relevance: Supports keeping K candidate hypotheses plus an execution check as default; does not isolate K or the S2 representation effect.

source: ARC Prize (2025) Which AI reasoning model is best? (leaderboard blog)
finding: Direct (no scaffold) reasoning models on ARC-AGI-1 semi-private set with cost per task. Page read through the fetch tool (summarised), numbers as relayed.
numbers: o3 (high) 60.8% at $0.50; o3-pro (high) 59.3% at $4.16; o4-mini (high) 58.7% at $0.406; Claude Sonnet 4 thinking 16k 40% at $0.366; Claude Opus 4 thinking 16k 35.7% at $1.25; Gemini 2.5 Pro 33.0% at $0.569; Gemini 2.5 Flash 33.3% at $0.037; DeepSeek R1 (5/28) 21.2%; GPT-4.1-nano 0%. o3-preview (low) 75.7% at $200.
quote: accuracy goes up as you stack these methods but efficiency goes way down
limits: Costs only, no token counts. Harness takes grids; page does not say whether models write code inside their reasoning.
agent_relevance: Baseline for the plain extended-reasoning arm: about 40-60% at $0.4-4 per task on ARC-AGI-1 for mid-2025 models.

source: Greenblatt (2024) Getting 50% (SOTA) on ARC-AGI with GPT-4o
finding: Sampling about 8,000 Python programs per task (about 5,000 initial plus 3,000 revisions) with example-based filtering and revision reached 50% on a 100-task test subset. Accuracy rose log-linearly, about 3 points per doubling of samples. Page read through the fetch tool.
numbers: Test 100 tasks: V0 1024 samples 25%; V1 27%; V1.1 28%; V2 30%; V2 at 2048 samples 34%; ensemble of four before revision 37%; with revision 50% (SE about 5). Held-out train subset 72% (cited human MTurk 85%). 37% with V0 alone would need about 43,000 samples; 50% with V2 alone about 100,000. Revision fixes about 20% of remaining wrong tasks; 3,040 revision samples per problem, only where fewer than 32 programs pass. Top-2 instead of top-3: 48% vs 50% on test.
quote: adding about 3 percentage points per doubling of k
limits: GPT-4o, 2024, not a reasoning model. No plain-CoT or o1 comparison (author: 'I don't have numbers for cutting reasoning'). No count of programs that pass examples but fail the test. No measured dollar cost.
agent_relevance: No knee seen up to 2048 samples; gain per doubling stays about +3 while cost doubles. Revision is worth far more than plain samples at the margin. Majority vote over passing programs is the selector.

source: Pourcel, Colas & Oudeyer (2025) SOAR: self-improving LMs for evolutionary program synthesis (ARC-AGI)
finding: One-shot program synthesis is weak even for strong models. Sampling plus execution-feedback refinement lets small open models beat much larger one-shot models. Search gain is logarithmic in budget and bounded by the base model.
numbers: ARC-test one-shot program synthesis: Qwen2.5-Coder 7B 1.0, 14B 1.0, 32B 1.5; Qwen-72B 1.75; Mistral-Large-2 2.5; GPT-4.1 8.0; Claude-4-Sonnet 20.75; o3-mini 38.25 (reasoners 33.0 and up). Sample-6k / Sample&Refine-6k / SOAR-6k: 14B 5.63/14.25/36.25; 32B 12.63/19.87/42.75; GPT-4.1 19.75/26.25/45.50. Half sampling plus half refinement beat all-sampling at every size. SOAR (fine-tuned on own search traces) peak 52.00% on ARC test with majority voting.
quote: search performance typically scales logarithmically with compute budget
limits: One-shot cells are code-writing with no search. Table text partly garbled in extraction; alignment checked against prose. Sample&Refine and SOAR not run on closed models. 6k programs per task is a large budget; total tokens not reported.
agent_relevance: At equal budget, splitting between sampling and execution-guided refinement beats pure sampling at every size tested. Weights are fine-tuned there, which we cannot do.

source: Pourcel et al. (2025) SOAR, diversity and plateau analysis
finding: Search alone plateaus with larger budget and larger model. Solution diversity on solved tasks falls across training iterations but stays high on unsolved tasks. Gains come from improving the sampler, not only adding samples.
numbers: Figures 4-6: plateau with model size and budget when the model is not updated (exact values only in plots). Peak 52.00% needed voting over all iterations. Diversity = mean pairwise embedding distance per task.
limits: Plateau values are in figures that were not readable as text. Relevant to training, not to a frozen scaffold.
agent_relevance: A frozen agent cannot self-train, but keep diversity on unsolved items and stop spending on solved ones (per-item stopping).

source: Ho et al. (2025) ArcMemo: abstract reasoning composition with lifelong LLM memory
finding: Same harness for all arms: the model writes a Python transform, runs it on demonstrations, gets execution feedback; ARC-AGI-1 100-puzzle validation subset; official 2 attempts. A frontier reasoning model (o4-mini medium) already reaches 55.17 with this propose-and-test loop. Concept memory adds a few points.
numbers: No-memory o4-mini: Oracle@1 46.33 (SD 1.04), official Oracle@2 55.17 (3.18), Oracle@3 59.50. ArcMemo-PS: 48.00 / 59.33 (0.29); ArcMemo-OE 56.67 (1.53); cheatsheet baseline 57.67 (2.52). Abstract: +7.5% relative gain over no-memory baseline. Other models on same harness (Oracle@2): Claude Sonnet 4 thinking 16k 54.17; DeepSeek R1 26.33; Qwen3-235B instruct 16.67; Gemini 2.5 Flash thinking 16k 13.83.
limits: Three runs; SD up to 3-5 points, so a 4-point gain is about one SD in noisy cells. Table text garbled in places; headline cells match prose. One benchmark subset. No direct-grid arm at equal tokens in this paper. Memory seeded with 160 human-written Python solutions from Li et al.
agent_relevance: Modern evidence that propose-code-and-execute with a frontier reasoning model is a strong baseline (55% at 2 attempts), and that abstract-concept memory gives small, consistent gains.

source: Ho et al. (2025) ArcMemo, compute scaling, continual update and token cost
finding: Memory advantage is biggest at low compute and shrinks as compute grows, because the model can rediscover ideas by exploring. Updating memory during the test run helps at high retry depth. Memory runs use as many or more output tokens, not fewer.
numbers: Abstract-concept memory (PS) was the only design above baseline at every tested compute scale. Continual update every 10 problems, ArcMemo-OE: 60.67 to 62.33 at @1 and 67.67 to 70.00 at @2 in one retry setting. Appendix C: token use 'similar to the baseline'; memory runs raised output tokens; authors guess the model explores more hypotheses and false positives are 'manageable by the reasoning models' at the cost of tokens.
quote: The marginal impact of memory is reduced with more inference compute
limits: Differences are small against SD of 1.5-3.5 points. Memory seeded with human solutions. Reuse of individual concepts judged qualitatively (concept coverage), not as a counted reuse rate.
agent_relevance: A memory of named abstractions can pay on a later batch, but modestly and mostly at low compute. Expect no token saving.

source: Berlot-Attwell, Rudzicz & Si (2024) Library learning doesn't: the curious case of the single-use library
finding: Re-analysis of LEGO-Prover and TroVE logs: learned functions are almost never reused, and removing cross-problem sharing barely hurts. Gains are better explained by self-correction and self-consistency.
numbers: LEGO-Prover: over 20,000 lemmas learned; only 1,233 (6%) entered the prover prompt; exactly one lemma reused verbatim, once; by name no lemma appeared in 3 or more solutions. Solved counts: valid+GPT 127, valid+Human 135, test+GPT 111, test+Human 122. Ablation without cross-problem sharing (GPT-4o-mini, 12-problem subset, 50 attempts, 2 trials) solved only 1 fewer problem. TroVE: 15 learned functions, 2 reused in correct solutions, 3 successful reuses in 3,201 test questions.
limits: Domains are theorem proving (miniF2F) and Python math/table QA, not ARC. Weak LLMs (GPT-3.5, 4o-mini). Small ablation (12 problems).
agent_relevance: Reconciles with LILO and ArcMemo: reuse as a literal function call is near zero in LLM agents; ArcMemo's gain comes from idea hints in the prompt (indirect reuse). Log both reuse rate and a no-memory control.

source: Lee et al. (2025) Generating Diverse Hypotheses for Inductive Reasoning (Mixture of Concepts), scaling table
finding: With GPT-4o-mini, accuracy of plain IID hypothesis sampling keeps rising with K up to 256 on four tasks (List Functions, MiniARC, MBPP+, Playgol-str). Concept-first diversity (MoC) gains most at small and middle K; the gain nearly vanishes at K=128.
numbers: Average test accuracy, baseline vs MoC (Table 8): K=4 36.1 vs 39.7; K=8 39.2 vs 43.7; K=16 42.7 vs 47.1; K=32 45.4 vs 47.8; K=64 49.0 vs 53.6; K=128 54.4 vs 54.7; K=256 55.0 vs 59.8. At K=32, split 16 concepts x 2 hypotheses: 52.0 (+6.6); 32x1: 47.8; 8x4: 48.9. Authors: MoC matches baseline with about half the hypotheses.
limits: Cost counted in hypotheses, not tokens: MoC adds a concept-proposal stage whose tokens are not charged to K. Weak model; MiniARC only 5-21%. Table layout garbled for some rows; K rows consistent with prose '+4.5 points for GPT-4o-mini'.
agent_relevance: No clear knee for IID sampling up to K=256 (only +0.6 from 128 to 256). Diversity prompting pays most at K of 4 to 32, worth roughly one to two doublings of K there.

source: Lee et al. (2025) Mixture of Concepts: temperature, refinement and cause of the gain
finding: Raising temperature raises diversity and accuracy only up to a point; text degeneration stops further gain. Iterative hypothesis refinement does not beat plain sampling with the weaker model. Authors say MoC's gain is mostly more diverse hypotheses, not better reasoning.
numbers: Best split of 32 hypotheses (GPT-4o-mini): 16 concepts x 2 per concept 52.0 average (+6.6 over baseline). With greedy decoding MoC shows no significant gain (Table 4). Iterative refinement (T=2,N=4) beat baseline for GPT-4o but not for GPT-4o-mini.
limits: One group, four tasks, models 4o-mini, 4o, Llama-3.1-70B, Qwen-2.5-72B; no reasoning model.
agent_relevance: A frontier reasoning model already diversifies inside its own reasoning; the gain from forced-diversity prompts there is untested. Run the K-sweep before adopting it.

source: Li et al. (2024) Combining Induction and Transduction for Abstract Reasoning, false positives and complementarity
finding: Fine-tuned Llama-3.1-8B induction and transduction models solve different ARC problems, and the split is stable across random seeds. About 9% of sampled programs that fit the training pairs give a wrong test output; for about half of the problems with false positives, most passing samples still predict the right output.
numbers: False-positive rate about 9% of passing samples; of problems with any, about half have a rate below 0.5. Induction solve rate rises almost monotonically up to 2,000 samples (Sample+Filter below Sample+Oracle). Ensemble: try induction first, fall back to transduction if no program passes. All models beat humans on the hardest 20% of problems and fall below humans on the easiest 20%.
limits: Fine-tuned 8B models on synthetic ARC-like data, not prompted frontier models; the 9% is for this generator. Per-row table layout garbled; 56.75% ensemble verified in prose earlier.
agent_relevance: Cheap check: majority vote across passing programs removes false positives in about half of affected problems at no extra test cost. Routing signal: induction first, transduction when nothing passes.

source: Qiu et al. (2024) Phenomenal Yet Puzzling: raw vs task accuracy gap
finding: Raw accuracy (per example) is far above task accuracy (all examples of a task right) when the LM predicts outputs directly. Applying the proposed rule through a symbolic interpreter narrows the gap on MiniSCAN but not on ACRE. Using the LM itself as interpreter makes things worse.
numbers: IO prompting, raw vs task: ACRE 64.0 vs 28.0; MiniSCAN 61.7 vs 0.0; List Fns 65.1 vs 39.6; MiniARC 33.1 vs 13.8. Refinement T=1,N=1: ACRE 78.2 vs 45.0; MiniSCAN 46.3 vs 0.0; List Fns 67.4 vs 52.0; MiniARC 5.9 vs 3.8. T=3,N=1: MiniSCAN 77.0 vs 46.0; ACRE 77.8 vs 47.0. Self-refine with LM as interpreter (T=3,N=5): MiniSCAN task 0.0.
quote: some correct predictions might be generated without using the expected computation
limits: Task accuracy is strict, so a gap is expected even for a faithful rule; the paper reads the gap as unfaithfulness only for direct prediction. Cells use different T,N. GPT-4-era model.
agent_relevance: Executing the rule in code makes the answer follow the rule by construction; the remaining raw-task gap is a partly wrong rule, not unfaithfulness.

source: Qiu et al. (2024) Phenomenal Yet Puzzling, MiniARC refinement failure
finding: Refinement lost on MiniARC raw accuracy. Authors suggest MiniARC items lean on pattern matching, where direct IO prompting is better, and note text-only models see grids poorly; a multimodal model did worse than text.
numbers: MiniARC raw accuracy: IO 33.1, SC(N=5) 31.3, SR 15.1, refinement T=1,N=1 5.9, T=1,N=5 12.8, T=3,N=1 10.1. Task accuracy: IO 13.8, SC 13.1, SR 9.2, T=1,N=1 3.8, T=1,N=5 9.2, T=3,N=1 6.9.
quote: some tasks in MiniARC are heavily dependent on pattern matching
limits: Explanation is the paper's guess, not tested. No router tested. One GPT-4-class model.
agent_relevance: Cheap signal to test: if no program among K proposals passes all demos, fall back to a direct answer (as in Li et al.) rather than trusting a refined program.

source: Xu, Li, Sanner & Khalil (2024) LLMs and the ARC: failures and object-based representations
finding: GPT-4 on text grids solved 13/50 of the simplest ARC tasks. Object-based description with a domain tool raised it to 23/50. The best representation on all 400 training tasks gave 81/400. Only weak models tested.
numbers: 13/50 direct grid to 23/50 object-based (+10 tasks); 81/400 solved on ARC training set with best representation; 20 of the 23 correct had correct reasoning per authors.
limits: GPT-4 only, no reasoning model, 50 easiest tasks. No 2025-26 model tested in any source opened. Survey's 20-30 point multi-representation advantage is uncontrolled.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 stays open: no controlled test of an object parse on o-series, Claude thinking or Gemini thinking was found. A per-item A/B (raw grid vs grid plus object list) is the only way to know.

source: Feldman (2000) Minimization of Boolean complexity in human concept learning (Nature 407:630-3), abstract
finding: Primary paper measured subjective difficulty over 41 mathematically distinct Boolean concept types in six families, far wider than earlier work. Difficulty was directly proportional to Boolean complexity, the length of the shortest equivalent propositional formula.
numbers: 41 concept types, 6 families. Law: difficulty proportional to Boolean complexity. N and correlation values are in the full text, which was paywalled and not read.
quote: the subjective difficulty of a concept is directly proportional to its Boolean complexity
limits: Abstract only (PubMed). Full-text numbers not checked. Lafond et al. 2007 abstract could not be retrieved (Crossref and PubMed had no usable record), so the contested part stays unverified.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 half closed: Feldman's claim confirmed from the abstract. No study found that regresses LLM item difficulty on shortest-formula length, so that agent test is new work.

source: Vahdati et al. (2026) The ARC of Progress towards AGI: A Living Survey of Abstraction and Reasoning (program libraries section)
finding: Survey says Pang's wake-sleep library learned 538 programs from 1,000 training tasks and cut LLM calls from 36 to 10 per task. Gain on ARC-AGI-2 still drops 2.5-3x.
numbers: Pang: 538 programs; calls per task 36 to 10; $3.97/task; ARC-AGI-1 77.1% to ARC-AGI-2 26.0%. Berman: 40 candidate instructions evolved per task, 79.6% at $8.42 to 29.4%.
limits: Second-hand summary of Substack posts, not peer reviewed; library reuse rate not given beyond the call reduction.
agent_relevance: A learned library can cut calls per task by about 70% on a same-distribution batch, a reuse-through-efficiency number; it did not carry to the harder ARC-AGI-2 distribution.
